subject: history
topic: Would you still obey? The Milgram experiment, repeated
angle: Modern replications show that obedience rates remain high, though identification with the science of the study and individual differences in empathy can influence behavior.
title: The Persistence of Obedience

hooks.text: You think you are different. The data says you are not.
You follow instructions because it is easier than choosing.
A hand reaches for a button.

reveal.headline: Obedience rates remain high in modern studies.
reveal.body: Participants in 2006 and 2017 replications showed levels of obedience similarly high to the original studies.,

explain.headline: Models of defiance do not stop you.
explain.body: Even when participants saw a confederate refuse instructions, they obeyed as often as those who saw no model at all.

matters.headline: Your identification with science matters.
matters.body: Those who identify less with the science of a study are more hesitant to press the button. That may be why your personal connection to a cause dictates your actions.

example.headline: The office manual.
example.body: You sit at your desk. You read a policy. You follow a step that feels wrong but is required by the company. You click the button.

verdict: The evidence confirms that high levels of obedience persist in modern replications, even when participants are aware the shocks are not real or when models of defiance are present.
caveat: Many modern studies are partial replications or use virtual reality because ethical considerations prevent full replications of the original experiments.
caption:
Obedience to authority is not a relic of the past. 

Modern replications show that high levels of obedience persist, even when participants see others refuse to comply. These studies are often partial replications due to ethical constraints. 

What is the first instruction you follow every day?
